qualitative_transfer_notes: Using a level estimate after an isolated spike may have damped changes in the forecast; this is a hypothesis, not an established cause.
A constant forecast may miss variation when the visible history is volatile or does not establish a stable level.
The dated text may not help forecast the series when its connection to the target is unclear or unverified.
Consider a robust level estimate when visible history contains an isolated extreme followed by values that appear to settle around a lower level.
Consider a flat forecast only when the visible history supports a stable level and provides no defensible trend or relevant covariates.
Treat dated text as contextual evidence only when its quality, timing, and relevance to the target can be assessed from prediction-time information.
Do not apply the level-estimate approach when visible history supports a sustained trend, recurring pattern, or changing level.
Do not use disaster-related text to adjust a forecast when its relevance to the target is unassessed or its sourcing is unverified.
Do not infer the target's meaning, unit, or the cause of an extreme value from this case.

Post-hoc case-local empirical update: The first B forecast anchored too low: aggregate validation residuals showed underprediction, while the series also contains rare upward excursions. Do not collapse to the lowest recent cluster or force a downward continuation. For an undefined target with a short volatile history, use a cautious central level that reflects the broader recent range, without trying to time an isolated spike.
